title: Idomeneo
facts: Idomeneo was a commission: in 1780 the Elector of Bavaria, Karl Theodor, asked Mozart and librettist Varesco for an opera for the Munich court carnival.
Listen to the end of the overture: its soft final chords are not a real ending but lead straight into G minor, the key of Ilia’s opening scene.
The opera premiered on 29 January 1781 at the Cuvilliés Theatre in Munich, conducted by Christian Cannabich.
The Munich press notice of the premiere didn’t mention Mozart by name. It raved about the sets instead, especially the view of the port and Neptune’s temple.
Idamante was written for a castrato. For a 1786 concert performance in Vienna, Mozart rewrote the part for a tenor.
Mozart fought with his librettist, the court chaplain Varesco, making big cuts and even changing words whose vowels the singers disliked, like the many i’s in “rinvigorir”.
Elettra’s “Tutte nel cor vi sento”: jealous of Ilia, she feels the furies of the underworld rising up in her heart.
This shipwreck scene closely follows the structure of a similar storm scene in Gluck’s Iphigénie en Tauride.
Saved from the storm, Idomeneo remembers his vow to Neptune: to sacrifice the first living creature he meets on land. It will be his own son.
Mozart wrote the title role for the tenor Anton Raaff, who sang it at the 1781 premiere. It was Raaff’s last stage role.
The critic Schubart thought Anton Raaff, the first Idomeneo, had the most beautiful male voice of all time.
C. F. D. Schubart (via Wikipedia, “Anton Raaff”)
In this intermezzo between Acts I and II, Cretan troops come off Idomeneo’s ship, their wives meet them, and everyone praises Neptune.
Mozart saves the piccolo for this one place in the opera: the storm in Act II.
“Zeffiretti lusinghieri”: alone in the royal garden, Ilia asks the breezes to carry her love to Idamante.
The three trombones play only here, to accompany the offstage Voice of Neptune.
Idomeneo was the first opera in which Mozart ended in the key of the overture, and he did so in all his later operas.
Despite all that work, Idomeneo was performed only three times in Munich.
Mozart also wrote about 15 minutes of ballet music (K. 367) for Idomeneo, which the Munich management requested. He reported on it in a letter to his father on 30 December 1780.
Later in 1781 Mozart considered making the opera more like Gluck, with a bass Idomeneo and a tenor Idamante, but he never did.
For the 150th anniversary in 1931, Richard Strauss made his own version for Vienna, replacing about a third of Mozart’s score with his own music.
The first US performance came only in 1947, at Tanglewood, produced by Boris Goldovsky.
In 2006 the Deutsche Oper Berlin cancelled a revival of Hans Neuenfels’s Idomeneo, citing an “incalculable security risk” over its added final scene.
This Jean-Pierre Ponnelle staging was the Met’s first production of Idomeneo. It opened on October 14, 1982, with Luciano Pavarotti in the title role.
Met Opera Archives, performance record CID 270240
Ponnelle framed the stage with classical Roman columns and a broad flight of steps, in front of changing backdrops of ruins inspired by Piranesi.
F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, 1982 (Met Opera Archives)
At the Met premiere, a critic wrote that Hildegard Behrens as Elettra “literally stopped the show” with this last-act aria.
F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, 1982 (Met Opera Archives)
The 1982 Washington Times review praised the opera’s two storm sequences, which it called perhaps the first realistic musical tempests in any opera.
F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, 1982 (Met Opera Archives)
